One classical statement, due to Clausius, is that heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder body to a hotter one. Kelvin's statement is that you cannot build an engine that turns heat entirely into work, in a cycle, with no other effect. The modern summary uses entropy: in an isolated system, entropy does not decrease. The statements are equivalent. They all say that some processes run one way and not the reverse, even when energy is conserved.

The first law is a conservation law. It would allow a cup of tea to get hotter while the room gets colder, if the energy books balanced. The second law is why that does not happen on its own. You can move heat from cold to hot, which is what a refrigerator does, but only by doing work and dumping even more heat somewhere else. The refrigerator plus the kitchen is not a counterexample. It is the law in action.
posts.deeper:
Entropy is not a mood called disorder, though that metaphor sometimes helps. In statistical mechanics it tracks how many microscopic arrangements correspond to a macroscopic state. Systems tend to evolve toward states that can happen in more ways. That is a tendency of isolated systems, with a probability so close to certainty for anything large that we treat it as a law.

Earth is not an isolated system. It receives a stream of energy from the Sun and radiates energy to space. A cell takes in low-entropy food and dumps heat and waste. Local order can increase. The books are kept by the surroundings. OpenStax's University Physics treats the second law in its own chapter, and the encyclopedia articles on the second law and on entropy are the right companions if the word 'disorder' has started to do too much work.
posts.example: Two blocks, one hot and one cold, are placed in contact inside an insulated box. Energy flows from hot to cold until the temperatures match. The reverse, a spontaneous un-mixing back into hot and cold, is compatible with conservation of energy and is not observed. A refrigerator between them can make the cold block colder, but only while a motor runs and the coils at the back warm the room by more than the cold block lost. Turn the motor off and the spontaneous direction returns. Nothing in the example requires the blocks to be 'messy' or 'tidy.' It requires an isolated pair, and a direction.

review.notes: Clausius and Kelvin statements and the entropy formulation match the standard presentation in OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, chapter 4, and the encyclopedia articles. The card is explicit that organisms are not isolated systems.

posts.title: A system at equilibrium pushes back
posts.hook: Le Chatelier’s principle says which way an equilibrium shifts. It does not say how fast, and a catalyst does not change the answer.
posts.body:
Henri Le Chatelier stated the idea in the 1880s. If a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partly counteracts the disturbance. Add more of a reactant and the system makes more product. Squeeze a gas mixture and it shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas. Heat an equilibrium and it shifts in the endothermic direction, the direction that absorbs heat.

The principle is qualitative. It tells you the direction of the shift, not the new concentrations, and not the time required. It also does not say the disturbance is completely undone. Add reactant and some of the addition is consumed, not all of it. A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor. Equilibrium arrives sooner and sits in the same place. Anyone who adds a catalyst expecting a new equilibrium has asked the principle to do a job it does not do.
posts.deeper:
The ammonia synthesis is the standard illustration, and it is worth keeping the names straight. Nitrogen and hydrogen form ammonia: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, with heat released. Four moles of gas become two, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium toward ammonia. Because the reaction is exothermic, a lower temperature also favours ammonia, but the reaction is then painfully slow. Industrial Haber–Bosch plants use high pressure, a compromise temperature, and a catalyst. Le Chatelier did not invent that process. Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch did, later. They were using equilibrium logic he had helped make obvious.

OpenStax Chemistry 2e, section 13.3, states the principle with these cases. The failure mode in student problems is almost always the catalyst, or a pressure change in a reaction where the number of gas moles does not change. If both sides have the same number of gas molecules, squeezing does not pick a side.
posts.example: Start with the ammonia equilibrium at a fixed temperature. Double the pressure by compressing the vessel. The mixture shifts toward ammonia, the side with fewer gas molecules, which brings the total pressure back down a little, not all the way. The new equilibrium has a higher mole fraction of ammonia. Now add a catalyst and change nothing else. The approach to that same equilibrium speeds up. The mole fraction you were heading toward does not move. Finally, raise the temperature. Because making ammonia releases heat, the hotter equilibrium contains less ammonia, even though the reaction is faster. Speed and position are different knobs.

sources.title: 13.3 Shifting Equilibria: Le Châtelier’s Principle, Chemistry 2e (OpenStax)

review.notes: The direction of shifts for concentration, pressure, and temperature, and the fact that a catalyst does not move the equilibrium, match OpenStax Chemistry 2e section 13.3. The ammonia equation is the standard illustration. Haber–Bosch is not attributed to Le Chatelier.

posts.title: There is no last prime number
posts.hook: Euclid’s proof does not say that one plus the product of the primes you listed is itself prime. It says that product-plus-one has a prime factor you missed.
posts.body:
A prime number is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. Euclid's Elements, Book IX, Proposition 20, proves that there are more primes than any finite list you can write down. Suppose the list p1, p2, ..., pk is every prime. Form N = p1 times p2 times ... times pk, plus 1. N is bigger than 1, so it has some prime factor. That factor cannot be any pi on the list, because dividing N by pi leaves a remainder of 1. So there is a prime that was not on the list. The supposition that the list was complete is false.

The proof never claims that N itself is prime. Often it is not. Two times three times five times seven times eleven times thirteen, plus one, equals 30031, and 30031 is 59 times 509. Both 59 and 509 are primes that were not in the opening list. That is all the argument needed.
posts.deeper:
The result is that the primes do not run out. It is not a recipe for generating the next prime, and it is not a statement about how dense the primes are. Much later mathematics, from Euler's product for the Riemann zeta function through the prime number theorem, describes that density. Euclid's proposition is earlier and more elementary, which is why it is still the right first proof.

The common slip, repeated in popular accounts, is to check a few cases where the product plus one happens to be prime (2+1, 2 times 3 plus 1, and so on) and to think the proof says this always happens. The fifth primorial-plus-one is already composite if you start from a longer list, and the proof is unbothered. David Joyce's online edition of the Elements states Proposition IX.20 in Euclid's form. Reading one translation alongside that slip is the whole lesson.
posts.example: Start with the list 2, 3, 5. The product plus one is 31, which is prime, so this particular case does hand you a new prime directly. Start with 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13. The product is 30030, plus one is 30031. Divide by 59: 59 times 509 is 30031. Neither 59 nor 509 was on the list, so the list was incomplete, exactly as the proof said, even though 30031 is not prime. If someone tells you Euclid proved that 'the product of the first k primes, plus one, is always prime,' the number 30031 is a sufficient reply.

sources.title: Euclid’s Elements, Book IX, Proposition 20 (David Joyce)

review.notes: Proposition IX.20 was checked against Joyce’s edition of the Elements. The composite example was recomputed: 2×3×5×7×11×13+1 = 30031 = 59×509. The card corrects the common claim that N itself must be prime.
corrections: The proof does not claim that one plus the product of the listed primes is prime. The published text says only that this number has a prime factor off the list, and gives 30031 = 59×509 as a counterexample to the stronger claim.

posts.title: A payment later is worth less than the same payment now
posts.hook: Present value is the number you would accept today in place of a future cash flow, once you have named a discount rate.
posts.body:
If money you hold can earn a return, then receiving 100 in a year is not the same as receiving 100 now. The 100 now could become 100 times (1 + r) in a year. So the future 100 is worth 100 / (1 + r) today. That is its present value at the discount rate r. Further away, you divide by (1 + r) once per year: PV = FV / (1 + r)^t.

The rate is doing a lot of quiet work. At a minimum it stands for the return you give up by waiting, which is why discounting is the other side of compound interest. It often also stands for risk: a payment that might not arrive is not discounted at the same rate as a treasury bill. Mixing those reasons up is how people argue past each other. One of them is talking about time. The other is talking about whether the payer will pay.
posts.deeper:
Add the present values of every promised cash flow and you have a price for a bond, a project, or a tuition plan, given your rates. Change the rate and the price moves. Long-dated cash flows move more, because the exponent is larger. A project that is mostly a big receipt in year 30 can look wonderful at 2 percent and ordinary at 8 percent, with no change in the receipt.

The formula does not choose the rate. That choice is the economics: the opportunity cost of capital for this kind of risk. A public agency discounting a bridge and an investor discounting a startup should not be forced to use the same number, because they are not giving up the same alternative. Present value is an organising identity. It becomes a valuation only after the rate is defended.
posts.example: You are offered 110 in one year, for certain, and you can lend or borrow safely at 10 percent. The present value is 110 / 1.10 = 100. Paying 100 today for that promise is a fair swap with the safe rate. Paying 105 is a loss: 105 would grow to 115.50 if you lent it yourself, which beats 110. Now suppose the 110 might fail. You do not repair that by pretending the rate is still 10 percent. You either cut the expected receipt (say a 50 percent chance, so 55 expected, present value 50 at the safe rate) or you raise the discount rate and say what risk premium you think you are using. The arithmetic will not choose for you. It will stop you from doing both corrections at once without noticing.

sources.title: Compound interest, Investor.gov (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

review.notes: The one-period example 110/1.10 = 100 was checked, as was the alternative growth of 105 at 10 percent to 115.50. The card separates the pure time discount from a risk adjustment.

posts.title: Every transaction is written down twice
posts.hook: Double-entry bookkeeping did not begin with Luca Pacioli. He wrote down, in 1494, a method Italian merchants were already using.
posts.body:
In a double-entry ledger, every transaction hits two accounts. One side is a debit, the other a credit, and the two amounts match. Sell goods for cash and the cash account rises while sales, or the stock you gave up, is recorded on the other side. The books are built so that they have to balance. The accounting equation that students still learn is the same idea in one line: assets equal liabilities plus equity.

Luca Pacioli, a Franciscan friar and mathematician, described the Venetian method in his Summa de arithmetica, published in Venice in 1494. He is often called the father of accounting. The fairer statement is that he codified a merchant practice and gave it a wide audience. The method was in use in Italian cities well before his book. Writing it down mattered because a written method can travel, and because a method that must balance makes some errors visible. It does not make fraud impossible. A dishonest bookkeeper enters the lie on both sides.
posts.deeper:
The historical interest is not the arithmetic, which is simple. It is what the arithmetic lets an organisation see. A merchant with a single list of receipts can lose track of what is owed and what is owned. A ledger that ties every inflow to a source, and every outflow to a use, can produce a statement of profit and a statement of position from the same records. That is a tool for partners who do not watch the shop every day, and later for investors who never visit it.

Historians argue about how much of European commercial growth to hang on the ledger. The safe claim is narrower and still interesting. By the end of the fifteenth century the method was articulate, teachable, and already older than its famous textbook. Pacioli's virtue was exposition, including a place in a much larger work of mathematics, not a flash of invention in 1494.
posts.example: A shop buys a table for 10 in cash. Cash falls by 10. Inventory, or equipment, rises by 10. The books balance, and profit is untouched: wealth changed shape, not size. The table is later sold for 15 in cash. Cash rises by 15, inventory falls by 10, and the difference of 5 is profit, which increases equity. Skip the second side of either entry and the books will not balance, which is the error-catching feature. Invent both sides, cash up 15 and a fake sale of 15, and the books balance while the profit is a fiction. The method checks arithmetic consistency. It does not check the world.

review.notes: Pacioli’s Summa of 1494 described an existing Italian merchant practice rather than inventing double entry. That correction of the popular ‘father of accounting’ line is in the card. The debit-credit example was checked against the accounting equation.
corrections: Rejected the claim that Pacioli invented double-entry bookkeeping. The published text says he codified Venetian practice in 1494.

posts.title: Winner-take-all districts tend toward two parties
posts.hook: Maurice Duverger’s ‘law’ is a tendency with a mechanism. It is not a rule that countries are obliged to obey.
posts.body:
Duverger argued, in work that reached English readers in the 1950s, that the way votes become seats shapes the party system. Where each district elects one person and the winner is whoever has the most votes, third parties are punished twice. Mechanically, a party spread thinly can win many votes and few seats. Psychologically, voters who expect that waste often abandon their first choice for a candidate who can win. Both effects push toward two parties that can actually take a district.

Proportional representation, which gives seats in rough proportion to votes, weakens both effects. A small party can turn votes into seats, so fewer voters feel they are wasting a ballot. More parties persist. That is the pairing Duverger is remembered for: plurality rules with two-party politics, proportional rules with more.
posts.deeper:
Calling it a law overstates the regularity. Canada has often had more than two parties under plurality rules. India has many. Regional parties can be large in one place and irrelevant nationally, which the district-level logic actually allows: a party that is first in Quebec or in a single state is not a wasted vote there. Presidential elections and social cleavages matter too.

The useful part is the pair of mechanisms, not the nickname. If you change the electoral rule, you change the penalty for being third. You do not thereby choose how many social divisions a country has. Researchers since Duverger have spent their time on the exceptions and on the size of the effects. A careful use of the idea predicts a pressure, and then goes looking for what else is holding the party system in place.
posts.example: A district of 100 voters splits 40, 35, 25 among three parties. Under plurality, the party with 40 takes the only seat. The 25 have no seat and, next time, some of them may vote for whichever of the larger two they dislike less. Under a proportional rule that allocated several seats by vote share, the third party would keep a foothold and the tactical reason to leave it would be weaker. Scale that up to a whole country of single-member districts and you can see a national third party lose everywhere while the two leaders collect seats. Scale it to a country where the third party is the local majority in a region, and Duverger's pressure does not erase it.

review.notes: The mechanical and psychological effects match the standard account of Duverger’s law. The card calls it a tendency and names Canada and India as cases where plurality rules have not produced a simple two-party system.

posts.title: The cost of a choice is the best thing you didn’t take
posts.hook: A free afternoon is not free if you had something else worth doing with it.
posts.body:
Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative you give up. It is not the sum of every alternative, and it is not the cash that leaves your pocket. Cash is part of the story only when spending it closes off something else you valued.

Economists use the idea to separate accounting profit from economic profit. Accounting profit counts explicit costs: wages, rent, materials. Economic profit also subtracts what the owner could have earned by using their time and capital in the next-best way. A shop can show an accounting profit and still be a poor use of the owner's afternoon, if that afternoon was worth more elsewhere. The cost was real. It just never appeared on the invoice.
posts.deeper:
The idea is older than the phrase. Once you take scarcity seriously, every yes is a no to something. The modern classroom version is tied to the production possibility frontier: points on the frontier price one good in units of the other. Moving along the frontier, the opportunity cost of more of one good is the amount of the other you stop producing.

Two limits matter. First, 'the' next-best alternative depends on what was actually available, not on a fantasy option. Second, people can be wrong about the value of what they gave up. The definition is about the best forgone alternative, not about whatever the chooser happened to dwell on. Sunk costs, already spent and unrecoverable, are not opportunity costs of going forward. That is the practical twin of the definition.
posts.example: A researcher is offered a paid workshop that fills an afternoon they would otherwise have spent finishing a paper. The ticket is waived, so the accounting cost is zero. The opportunity cost is the value of the progress on the paper, if that was the best other use of the afternoon. If the paper was worth more than the workshop, the free ticket was expensive. Reverse the values and the workshop is cheap even with a fee, up to the point where the fee plus the lost afternoon exceeds the workshop. The invoice and the opportunity cost answer different questions.

review.notes: The definition matches the standard textbook notion: the value of the next-best forgone alternative, distinct from accounting cost and from sunk cost. No numerical claim beyond the illustrative afternoon was added.

posts.title: Light below a threshold frequency ejects no electrons
posts.hook: Turn up the brightness of light that is too red, and a metal still emits nothing. Einstein’s 1905 account said the energy arrives in packets.
posts.body:
Shine light on a metal and, in the right conditions, electrons come off. Classical wave theory expected two things that do not happen. Brighter light, of any colour, should eventually shake electrons loose, and the energy of those electrons should rise with brightness. What happens instead: below a threshold frequency, no electrons leave, however bright the beam. Above the threshold, brighter light means more electrons, not faster ones. The kinetic energy of the fastest electrons rises with the frequency of the light.

Einstein's 1905 explanation was that light delivers energy in quanta, later called photons, each of energy E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is the frequency. An electron is ejected only if one quantum supplies at least the energy needed to leave the metal, the work function. Extra energy becomes kinetic energy. A brighter beam is more quanta, not bigger ones. The Nobel Prize awarded to Einstein for 1921 cited this law of the photoelectric effect, not relativity.
posts.deeper:
The result was one of the empirical doors into quantum theory. It does not, by itself, say everything about what light is. Later quantum electrodynamics treats light as having both wave and particle aspects in a more precise way. Historically, the photoelectric effect was decisive because it was so specifically unlike a classical wave. Robert Millikan confirmed the predicted linear relation between frequency and electron energy, and said he had tried to refute it.

The practical descendants include photomultipliers and the sensors in cameras, which count absorbed quanta. None of that requires the popular shortcut 'light is particles, so waves were a mistake.' Interference is still real. The photoelectric effect constrains how energy is exchanged. OpenStax University Physics, volume 3, section 6.2, walks through the observations without the shortcut.
posts.example: Suppose a metal needs 2 electronvolts to release an electron. A photon with 1.5 electronvolts cannot pool with its neighbours in this mechanism. A million of them, arriving as a brighter beam, still each fall short, and no electrons leave. A photon with 3 electronvolts can release an electron and leave it with up to about 1 electronvolt of kinetic energy. Double the brightness of that higher-frequency light and you roughly double the number of electrons, while the maximum kinetic energy stays put. The numbers here are illustrative. The pattern, a threshold in frequency and a slope in energy versus frequency, is the measured one.

review.notes: The threshold-frequency facts and E = hf match OpenStax and the standard account. The Nobel citation for 1921 was the photoelectric effect, as the Nobel facts page records. The 2 eV numbers are labelled as an illustration.

posts.title: Parallel lines meet at a point you choose
posts.hook: Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective in Florence in the early fifteenth century. The panel is lost. What survives is the geometry, written up by Alberti in 1435.
posts.body:
Linear perspective is a method for constructing a picture so that lines which are parallel in the world, and perpendicular to the picture plane, converge to a vanishing point. Objects of equal size are drawn smaller as they recede, in a ratio fixed by the geometry of one viewpoint. The picture is what a single eye, at a single spot, would see projected onto a plane.

Filippo Brunelleschi, in Florence in the early fifteenth century, demonstrated the method with panels of the Baptistery and the Palazzo Vecchio. The panels are lost. We know the demonstration from Antonio Manetti's biography, written later. Leon Battista Alberti's De pictura (1435) is the treatise that states the construction so a painter can carry it out: a horizon, a vanishing point, and a way of spacing the receding intervals. The geometry spread through European painting because it could be taught, not because everyone agreed it was the only honest way to paint.
posts.deeper:
Perspective solves one problem, the consistent projection from one viewpoint. It does not solve every problem a picture has. A wide scene forces a choice of where the viewer stands, and the edges of a very wide view look stretched if you insist on one plane and one point. Medieval and many non-European traditions constructed space by other rules: stacked registers, oblique parallel lines that do not meet, or a focus organised by importance rather than by optics. Those are systems, not failed attempts at Alberti.

There is also a gap between the construction and the eye. We have two eyes, we move, and we do not experience the world as a perspective diagram. The diagram is a convention that matches a projection. It was a powerful convention for architecture, stage design, and painting that wanted that match. Calling it 'how humans see' is a step further than the geometry goes.
posts.example: Stand on a straight road. The edges of the road are parallel on the ground and appear to meet near the horizon, at the vanishing point. A row of equal lamp posts along the road should be drawn so that their tops and bases lie on lines meeting at that same point, and the gaps between them shrink in a determined way, not by feel. Alberti's construction tells you where the next gap goes. Move the viewpoint closer and the nearest post grows sharply relative to the far ones. That sensitivity to the viewpoint is the method working. A picture that converges the road to one point and lets the lamp posts wander off a different point is not 'expressive perspective.' It is two viewpoints in one drawing, and the road will look bent whether or not you meant it to.

review.notes: Alberti’s De pictura of 1435 and Brunelleschi’s early-fifteenth-century demonstrations, known through Manetti, match the standard art-historical account. The card does not treat linear perspective as the only coherent pictorial system.

posts.title: A colour changes when its neighbour changes
posts.hook: Michel-Eugène Chevreul, a chemist at the Gobelins tapestry works, showed that some complaints about dyes were complaints about vision.
posts.body:
Simultaneous contrast is the shift in a colour's appearance caused by a colour next to it, at the same time. A grey patch looks lighter on a black ground than on a white one. A colour pushes its neighbour toward the complementary hue: a grey beside green looks faintly reddish, a grey beside red looks faintly greenish. The dye did not change. The comparison did.

Chevreul was director of dyes at the Gobelins manufactory in Paris. Weavers complained that some blacks and some colours looked dull or wrong depending on the threads beside them. He showed that the chemistry was often fine and the perception was lawful. His book, De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs, appeared in 1839. Painters, including Georges Seurat later in the century, read him. The result is a piece of physiology that arrived through a factory.
posts.deeper:
Chevreul distinguished simultaneous contrast from successive contrast, which is the afterimage you see after staring at a colour and looking away. Simultaneous contrast happens while both colours are in view. It is not a small effect confined to a laboratory grey. Textile design, painting, and any interface that puts a coloured badge on a coloured ground are inside it. Two brands can use the same ink and look different because the field around the ink differs.

The principle does not say that colour is an illusion and therefore arbitrary. It says appearance is relational. If you care about the appearance, you have to specify the neighbour. Chevreul's practical advice to the weavers was about choosing combinations that would still look like the intended colour once the neighbours were present. That is a more useful moral than 'colour isn't real.' The chemistry of the dye and the physiology of the edge are both real, and they answer different complaints.
posts.example: Cut two squares from the same grey paper. Place one on a black sheet and one on a white sheet. The grey on black looks lighter. Nothing about the paper changed between the two placements, which you can check by swapping them and watching the appearance move with the ground rather than with the piece of paper. Then place a small grey square on a strong green. The grey takes on a rosy cast. Place the same square on a strong red and the cast goes the other way. A tapestry weaver seeing a black look brownish next to a blue has the same kind of problem Chevreul was hired to solve. Re-dyeing the black is the wrong first experiment. Changing, or accounting for, the neighbour is the right one.

review.notes: Chevreul’s role at the Gobelins and the 1839 book on simultaneous contrast match the standard account. The grey-on-black versus grey-on-white demonstration is the usual classroom illustration of lightness contrast. Seurat is named as a later reader, not as a pupil.

posts.title: Credit in science tends to flow to the already known
posts.hook: Robert Merton named it after a verse in Matthew: to those who have, more will be given. He was talking about reputation, not money alone.
posts.body:
In a 1968 paper in Science, Merton argued that the reward system of science does not only pay for the work. It pays an extra dividend to people who are already eminent. When a famous scientist and a less famous one make a similar contribution, the famous one tends to get a larger share of the recognition. The gap then compounds. Invitations, students, the benefit of the doubt in a dispute, and the chance to do the next visible piece of work flow toward the name people already know.

He called this the Matthew effect, after the Gospel line about more being given to those who have. The interviews he drew on, conducted by Harriet Zuckerman with Nobel laureates, were full of scientists describing exactly that tilt, sometimes as beneficiaries and sometimes as the people whose early work had been overlooked until a bigger name touched it.
posts.deeper:
The mechanism is not a conspiracy and it is not only unfairness, though it is often unfair. Readers use reputation as a filter because they cannot read everything. A famous co-author is easier to remember than the junior partner. Journals and prize committees are made of readers. The filter then changes the future, because recognition buys time and collaborators. Merton's point is that a system which looks like it rewards contributions one by one can still produce cumulative advantage.

Later work has looked for the effect in citations, hiring, and funding, with mixed sizes and plenty of argument about measurement. The 1968 paper is not a claim that every prize is undeserved, or that unknown scientists never break through. It is a claim about a bias in the allocation of credit, strong enough that the history of who 'made' a discovery is a poor photograph of who did the work.
posts.example: Two labs publish similar findings a few months apart. The lab led by a prizewinner is cited as the one that 'showed' the result. The other is cited, if at all, as 'see also.' Next year the prizewinner's lab is asked to write the review, which cites its own paper first, and a student who wants to enter the field writes to that lab. The second lab's paper was not worse. The returns went to the name that already organised other people's attention. Merton's effect is that loop. It can start from a genuine early difference and then run far past it.

sources.title: Robert K. Merton, “The Matthew Effect in Science,” Science (1968)

review.notes: The PDF is Merton’s Science paper, volume 159, pages 56–63, 5 January 1968, and it discusses Zuckerman’s interviews with Nobel laureates. The card stays with the credit-allocation claim and does not invent a measured size for the effect.

posts.title: Heritable variants that leave more offspring become common
posts.hook: Natural selection is a filter on variation that already exists. The variation is undirected. The filter is not a coin toss.
posts.body:
Three conditions do the work. Individuals vary. Some of that variation is heritable, so offspring resemble the parents that had it. And some variants leave more offspring than others, because of how they interact with the environment. If all three hold, the variants that reproduce better become a larger share of the next generation. That is natural selection. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace both arrived at it. Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) is the book that laid out the case.

Mutation and recombination supply variation. They do not aim at what would be useful. Selection is the part that is not random: which variants spread depends on their consequences for survival and reproduction in that environment. 'Survival of the fittest' was Herbert Spencer's phrase, and it is easy to turn into a tautology. The content is differential reproductive success of heritable variants, which you can in principle measure.
posts.deeper:
Selection is not the only process that changes the frequency of a variant. Drift, the luck of finite numbers, matters more when populations are small. Migration moves variants between populations. A trait can spread because it is tied to another trait that selection favours. And 'the fittest' is not a moral rank. It is a count of offspring in a stated environment, which can change when the environment changes.

Darwin did not know Mendel's mechanism of inheritance, which is why his account of how variation is passed on is the dated part of the book. The twentieth century joined genetics to selection in what biologists call the modern synthesis. The conditions above are still the ones to check when someone claims that a trait 'evolved for' a purpose. Purpose is a description you earn after the differential reproduction is shown, not a substitute for it.
posts.example: A population of beetles includes a heritable shade difference, dark and light, on a pale sandy background. Birds eat the beetles they see. Light beetles are eaten less often and, on average, leave more offspring. The next generation has a higher fraction of light beetles, even though nobody needed a new mutation that year and no beetle tried to change colour. Move the same population onto dark volcanic soil and the advantage can reverse. The filter changed. The inheritance did not suddenly become random, and it did not suddenly become a plan.

sources.title: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (Project Gutenberg)

review.notes: The three conditions match the standard statement of natural selection and Darwin’s argument in the Origin. The card separates selection from mutation, names Wallace, and does not treat ‘survival of the fittest’ as Darwin’s definition.

posts.title: A true belief can be justified and still not knowledge
posts.hook: Edmund Gettier needed three pages to show that 'justified true belief' is not yet a definition of knowledge.
posts.body:
For a long time, a tidy proposal looked enough: you know something when you believe it, it is true, and you have a good justification. In 1963 Gettier published two short cases where all three hold and, by almost everyone's lights, the person still does not know.

In the first case, Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job, and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket. Smith concludes that the person who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. In fact Smith gets the job, and Smith also happens to have ten coins. The belief is true. The evidence really did justify it. But the truth arrived by a coincidence the evidence was not about. The justification and the fact missed each other.
posts.deeper:
The paper is aimed at the analysis of knowledge, not at scepticism. Gettier does not say we know nothing. He says a popular analysis counts some lucky beliefs as knowledge. The second case in the paper uses a similar trick with a disjunction: a justified false belief, or-ed with a truth the believer has no evidence for, can still be a justified true belief.

Later work tried to patch the analysis. Some add a 'no false lemmas' rule. Some require the belief to be caused by the fact in the right way. Some, following Timothy Williamson, give up the project of defining knowledge out of simpler parts and take knowledge as basic. The cases survive as a test. If your theory says Smith knows, it has not met the problem Gettier posed.
posts.example: Suppose you look at a clock that stopped exactly twelve hours ago. It reads 4:00, and it is 4:00. You are justified in trusting the clock, and your belief is true. You do not know the time. The stopped clock is a cousin of Gettier's cases: a reliable-looking route, a true belief, and a success that is accidental relative to that route. Gettier's own case is sharper because the justification is genuine evidence about Jones, not a broken instrument. The accident is in which fact makes the belief true.

sources.title: The Analysis of Knowledge, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

review.notes: The case matches Gettier's first example as presented in the Stanford Encyclopedia entry on the analysis of knowledge. The stopped-clock story is labelled as a cousin, not as Gettier's own text.

posts.title: No program can decide whether every program halts
posts.hook: Alan Turing’s 1936 result is narrow and absolute. There is no general method that looks at an arbitrary program and an arbitrary input and always says, correctly, whether it will finish.
posts.body:
Some programs halt. Some run forever. It would be useful to have a checker, call it H, that takes the text of a program and an input and answers 'halts' or 'runs forever,' correctly, every time. Turing showed that no such H can exist, if the programs in question are as general as a Turing machine, which is as general as ordinary programming languages.

The argument is a diagonal trick. Suppose H exists. Build a program D that calls H on D's own text, and then does the opposite of what H predicted: if H says D halts, D loops forever; if H says D loops, D halts. Run D. Whatever H answered, D has done the other thing. So H was wrong about this one case. The supposition that a perfect H exists is false. Particular programs can still be analysed. Compilers prove that some loops terminate. The theorem is about a single method that works for every program and every input.
posts.deeper:
The result belongs to the decision problems of the 1930s. Hilbert had asked for a procedure that would decide the truth of any mathematical statement. Turing, and Alonzo Church by another route, showed that even the special question 'does this computation finish?' is already undecidable. Gödel's incompleteness theorem is a cousin, not the same theorem. One is about proofs in arithmetic. The other is about the non-existence of an algorithm.

Nothing here says computers cannot solve problems, or that software is mysterious. It says a certain universal tool is impossible, in the way a method for squaring the circle with straightedge and compass is impossible. You can still square lots of practical regions. You can still prove that your particular loop ends. You cannot write the checker that never fails. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entries on Turing and on Turing machines state the model. The halting problem is the application people remember.
posts.example: Imagine H as a function that has never been wrong. D is a short program: ask H whether D halts, and if the answer is yes, enter an infinite loop; if the answer is no, stop immediately. There is no consistent answer for H to give about D. This is not a bug in D. It is a proof that the specification of H cannot be met. A practical timeout is not a counterexample. A timeout that says 'I gave up' has not decided. A timeout that says 'this loops' will be wrong about a program that would have halted on step one more than the timeout allowed. The theorem is about correct answers, not about useful approximations.

sources.title: Turing machines, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
Alan Turing, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

review.notes: The diagonal construction matches the standard proof of the undecidability of the halting problem, as presented in the Stanford Encyclopedia entries on Turing and Turing machines. The card limits the claim to a general decider and does not say that particular programs cannot be analysed.

posts.title: Some arithmetic truths are not provable inside the system
posts.hook: Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem is a precise limit on formal proofs. It is not a slogan about truth being impossible.
posts.body:
In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved a theorem about formal systems that are strong enough to talk about basic arithmetic of the natural numbers. If such a system is consistent, meaning it does not prove a contradiction, then it is incomplete. There is a statement in its language that is true in the ordinary sense of arithmetic and that the system does not prove. The system cannot be both consistent and complete for that arithmetic.

The second incompleteness theorem is the sharper political fact inside mathematics. A consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency. You can prove the consistency of a weaker system by stepping outside it and using stronger methods. You cannot, from inside, finish the job with the system's own rules and still be sure, by those rules alone, that the system is consistent. 'Sure' here means a formal proof, not a feeling of confidence.
posts.deeper:
The popular retellings go wrong in a few standard ways. Gödel did not show that mathematics is contradictory. Consistency is an assumption of the first theorem, and the conclusion is incompleteness, which is a different fault. He did not show that nothing can be known, or that proof is useless. Arithmetic still proves infinitely many things. He showed that truth in the standard model of arithmetic outruns what any one such formal system can derive.

'Strong enough' is a real hypothesis. A very weak system can be complete for the small language it has, and useless for general arithmetic. The theorem is about systems that can represent the basic operations and reasoning we actually use with whole numbers. The Stanford Encyclopedia's entry on the incompleteness theorems is the right place to see the hypotheses stated with care. The 1931 paper is the primary text. Neither says that reason has collapsed.
posts.example: Think of a rulebook for proving claims about whole numbers, powerful enough to do ordinary arithmetic and consistent in fact. Gödel's construction builds, from the rulebook, a sentence that in effect says 'this sentence is not provable in this rulebook.' If the rulebook proved that sentence, it would be proving something false, and a system that proves a false arithmetic sentence of this kind is inconsistent. So, if it is consistent, it does not prove the sentence. But then the sentence is true: it really is not provable. Truth and provability-in-this-one-system come apart for that sentence. A different, stronger rulebook might prove it. That stronger book then has a sentence of its own.

sources.title: Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

review.notes: The statement follows the Stanford Encyclopedia: a consistent formal system capable of basic arithmetic is incomplete, and such a system cannot prove its own consistency. The card explicitly rejects the claim that Gödel showed mathematics to be contradictory.

posts.title: What comes to mind feels more common
posts.hook: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman argued that people estimate frequency by how easily examples arrive. Ease of recall is not frequency.
posts.body:
The availability heuristic is a shortcut: when you judge how often something happens, you reach for examples, and you let the ease of the reach stand in for the count. Vivid, recent, or widely reported events are easy to retrieve. Ordinary events are not. The shortcut is often good enough. It fails when ease and frequency come apart.

A classic demonstration in their work asked whether English has more words starting with the letter K or more words with K as the third letter. Starting words (kite, king, keep) come to mind quickly. Third-letter words are harder to search for, so people say the starting words are more common. In fact the third-letter words are more common. The judgement followed availability, not the dictionary. Their 1974 Science paper, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases,' put this shortcut beside two others, representativeness and anchoring. Kahneman's 2002 Nobel lecture is a later map of the same research, done with Tversky.
posts.deeper:
The practical stakes are in risk. A dramatic accident that leads the news is available. The uneventful journeys are not. People can then rank dangers in something closer to the order of headlines than the order of rates. The heuristic does not mean anyone is foolish for remembering the headline. It means the headline is a biased sample of the events, and a mind that uses memory as a sample inherits the bias.

Availability is also not the same as a careful statistical argument from the examples you have. A doctor who has just seen three cases of a rare disease, and who updates too far, is being tugged by availability. A doctor who knows the base rate and uses the cases as evidence is doing something else, closer to the update Bayes described. The heuristic is what you do instead of that arithmetic when the arithmetic is unavailable and the examples are not.
posts.example: Ask someone whether more people die in fires or by drowning in a given country, and do not let them look it up. Whichever cause they have seen on screen lately will feel larger. The feeling is information about their memory, not about the registry of deaths. The letter-K task is cleaner because the truth is in the dictionary and the bias has a direction you can predict before you run the experiment: the easier search will be judged more frequent. Tversky and Kahneman's claim is that this substitution, ease for frequency, is a general habit, not a trick confined to letters.

review.notes: The K-as-first-versus-third-letter demonstration and the 1974 heuristics paper are the standard account of availability, also covered in Kahneman’s Nobel lecture. The card does not attach a specific death-rate comparison, which would need its own source.

posts.title: Averages settle into a bell, even when the raw data do not
posts.hook: The central limit theorem is why a mean of many independent pieces looks normal. It has hypotheses. Infinite variance is one way to escape it.
posts.body:
Take independent observations from the same distribution, and assume that distribution has a finite mean and a finite variance. Add them up, or take their average, and standardise so the result has mean zero and variance one. As the number of observations grows, the distribution of that standardised average gets closer to the normal bell curve. The original distribution does not have to be a bell. A die is flat. The average of many dice is not.

That is the central limit theorem, in the form used all over applied statistics. It is why a sample mean has a standard error, and why confidence intervals that lean on a normal approximation are often decent for large samples even when each data point is skewed. 'Large' is not a universal number. A very skewed distribution takes longer to settle than a mild one. The theorem says where the sequence is going. It does not say your sample of thirty has arrived.
posts.deeper:
The finite-variance hypothesis is the one people drop without noticing. A Cauchy distribution is a textbook case with a defined centre and no finite variance. The average of Cauchy observations does not settle to a normal curve. It stays Cauchy. Heavy tails in real data are a reason to be slower with a normal approximation, not a reason to quote the theorem louder.

Independence matters too. If the observations share a common shock, you do not have n pieces of information. You may have something closer to one shock, repeated. The theorem is a gift to anyone averaging genuinely many, weakly dependent, finite-variance pieces. It is not a claim that everything in nature is normally distributed. Heights of adults are roughly bell-shaped for biological reasons. The theorem is about averages, not about the histogram of the raw world.
posts.example: One fair die shows 1 through 6 with equal probability. The shape is flat, the mean is 3.5, and the variance is finite. Roll thirty dice and average them. You will almost never see an average near 1 or near 6, because that would require nearly every die to cooperate. Averages near 3.5 pile up. Plot those averages over many rounds and the histogram looks like a bell, even though no single roll did. The theorem is the promise that this is not a special fact about dice. Replace the die with any independent draw that has a finite variance, take enough of them, and the standardised average does the same thing.

review.notes: The statement includes independent, identically distributed observations with finite mean and variance, and the Cauchy counterexample when variance is infinite. That matches the standard theorem as given by MathWorld and the encyclopedia account.

posts.title: Ice ages keep time with Earth’s orbit
posts.hook: Eccentricity, tilt, and wobble change how sunlight is distributed. NASA is explicit that this clock does not explain the warming of the last century.
posts.body:
Milutin Milankovitch calculated how three slow cycles change the sunlight reaching Earth. Eccentricity is the stretch of the orbit, on a rhythm near 100,000 years. Obliquity is the tilt of the axis, near 41,000 years. Precession is the wobble of that axis, on the order of 20,000 years. Together they do not much change the total sunlight the planet receives. They change where and in which season it arrives, and the northern continents are sensitive to summer sunlight, because a cool summer fails to melt the previous winter's snow.

The pacemaker paper of Hays, Imbrie, and Shackleton in 1976 found those rhythms in the climate record of ocean sediments. The match is the reason the cycles are taken seriously as a clock for the ice ages of the last few million years. NASA's account of the cycles states the three periods and the link to ice sheets.
posts.deeper:
A clock is not a complete cause. Ice sheets themselves change the climate, by reflecting sunlight and by altering the ocean and the carbon cycle, so the orbital nudge is amplified. The cycles also do not line up with every climate shift in Earth's deeper history, when the continents were elsewhere and the atmosphere was different. They are a theory about a particular era's ice ages.

They are not a theory of the warming measured since the late nineteenth century. That warming is fast compared with the orbital periods, and the orbital changes over the last few decades are far too small, and in the wrong pattern, to account for it. NASA's Milankovitch page says outright that the cycles cannot explain Earth's current warming. A card about the ice ages owes that sentence in the same breath as the 100,000-year rhythm.
posts.example: Tilt is the easiest of the three to picture. More tilt means hotter summers and colder winters in a hemisphere. Less tilt means milder seasons. A landmass in the north, with milder summers, keeps snow more easily, and an ice sheet can grow even if global annual sunlight barely changed. Precession decides which hemisphere has its summer when Earth is slightly closer to the Sun. Eccentricity decides how much that closer-farther difference matters. Stack a low-tilt, snow-friendly north on top of the right precession and a stretch of eccentricity, and you have the kind of configuration the pacemaker paper found written into the sediments. None of those cycles completes in a human lifetime. That is the simplest reason they cannot be the warming on a graph of the last hundred years.

sources.title: Milankovitch orbital cycles and Earth’s climate, NASA Science

review.notes: The three cycles and their approximate periods match NASA’s Milankovitch page, which also states that the cycles cannot explain current warming. Hays, Imbrie, and Shackleton 1976 is the standard ‘pacemaker’ citation. Periods are given as approximate.

posts.title: Design it stronger than the load you expect
posts.hook: A factor of safety is failure load divided by working load. The number is chosen, not discovered. An elevator and a bookshelf should not share it.
posts.body:
If a component fails at a load F and you intend to run it at a load W, the factor of safety is F/W. Equivalently, the allowable load is the failure load divided by the factor you chose. A cable that breaks at 10 kilonewtons, designed with a factor of 5, is given a working load of 2 kilonewtons. The extra capacity is there because the failure load is uncertain, the real load is uncertain, the material has flaws, and the consequences of being wrong are not all the same.

There is no universal correct factor written in the physics. Codes and experience set them. A static bookshelf bracket and a cable that carries people do not get the same number, because the uncertainty and the cost of failure differ. Using a larger factor is not free. The part gets heavier and more expensive. Engineering is the argument about how much margin this particular uncertainty is worth.
posts.deeper:
The simple ratio hides a few distinctions that matter once you design anything real. Failure can mean breaking, or it can mean bending too far to be useful. The load can be a steady weight or a repeated cycle that causes fatigue at a level a single pull would never reach. The failure load you put in the numerator may be a tested minimum, or a published average you should not trust. Modern structural practice often talks about load factors and resistance factors separately, rather than one lumped number. The lumped number is still the right introduction, because it makes the margin visible.

A factor of 1 means you believe your load and your strength exactly, and you accept failure at the first surprise. Almost no responsible design does that. A very large factor can be a way of refusing to measure the load. The interesting designs are the ones that say what uncertainty they bought the margin for.
posts.example: A hoist cable is tested to break at 10 kilonewtons. The heaviest intended load, including the box and a dynamic bump when the motor starts, is estimated at 1.6 kilonewtons, and the designer adds a further allowance and sets the working load at 2 kilonewtons. The factor of safety is 10/2 = 5. If someone then hangs 4 kilonewtons on it, the factor on the day is 2.5, not 5. The printed factor was a statement about the design load, not a property that travels with the cable into every misuse. If a later test shows that some cables from the batch break at 8 rather than 10, the honest factor on the original design load falls to 4, and the code, not the slogan, decides whether 4 is still enough for a hoist that carries people.

review.notes: The definition, failure load over working load, matches the standard engineering usage. The 10 kN and factor-of-5 arithmetic gives a 2 kN working load and was checked. The card states that codes, not a law of nature, choose the factor.

posts.title: A null model for when gene frequencies stay put
posts.hook: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is what happens when nothing interesting is happening to the genes. Its use is to notice when something is.
posts.body:
Take a gene with two alleles, A and a, at frequencies p and q, with p + q = 1. If mating is random and nothing is systematically adding, removing, or favouring either allele, then the genotype frequencies in the next generation are p² for AA, 2pq for Aa, and q² for aa. Those three add to 1. Allele frequencies stay at p and q. The population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

G. H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg published the result independently in 1908. It answered a worry that dominant alleles would inevitably take over. They don't, not from dominance alone. A rare recessive allele spends most of its time hidden in heterozygotes, and its frequency is stable under the assumptions. The equation is a null model. If you measure genotypes and they are far from p², 2pq, q², then at least one assumption has failed. The equation does not say which one.
posts.deeper:
The assumptions are the content. No selection. No mutation that matters at this gene. No migration that brings alleles in or out. Random mating, rather than mates chosen by genotype. And a population large enough that chance, drift, does not shove the frequency around. Real populations violate these in various combinations. That is why the model is a baseline rather than a description of a forest.

People also confuse genotype frequency with allele frequency. If 1 percent of people show a recessive condition, that is q², not q. The allele can be much more common than the condition, because most copies sit in carriers. Screening programmes and textbook problems both start from that square root. OpenStax Biology 2e, section 19.2, is the classroom version. It is worth reading beside the assumptions, not instead of them.
posts.example: Suppose a recessive allele has frequency q = 0.1, so p = 0.9. Under the assumptions, the fraction of people who are aa, and who show the recessive trait if it is fully recessive, is q² = 0.01, one percent. Carriers, Aa, are 2pq = 2 times 0.9 times 0.1 = 0.18, eighteen percent. AA is 0.81. Most copies of the rare allele are in the eighteen percent, not in the one percent who are affected. If you then observe that almost nobody is a carrier and almost everyone is aa, the numbers are nowhere near this, and you go looking for selection, non-random mating, or a population that is not mixing. You do not 'fix' the algebra.

review.notes: The genotype frequencies p², 2pq, and q² and the 1908 attribution match the standard statement. The example was recomputed: q = 0.1 gives q² = 0.01 and 2pq = 0.18. The card treats the equation as a null model.
